issues.item: Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
issues.explanation: 'Irritability' is not a threat appraisal/perception item; it reflects arousal/behavioral dysregulation and fits better outside the Threat node. In this profile, the other Threat items are coherent terrorism-related hypervigilance/safety behaviors ('Scanning Exits', 'Back to Wall'), so this item is internally mismatched within the node and weakly aligned with the formulation in which Memory-linked threat should reflect perceived current danger rather than aggressive behavior.

vignette:
Kwame, a 33-year-old tailor, built his life around the hum of his sewing machine and the bustling energy of the marketplace where his small shop stood. That changed irrevocably on a sweltering afternoon when the market exploded into chaos. A sudden, deafening blast shattered the air, followed by screams and the terrifying thud of falling debris. Kwame remembers the sheer terror, the scramble for safety, but large parts of the event remain a blur; there are significant memory gaps he simply cannot access, no matter how desperately he tries to piece it together. Other times, the memory plays like a relentless, looping film, a vivid memory replay of the most frightening moments – the dust, the cries, the overwhelming sense of doom. Yet, strangely, at other times he can recall what happened with an unsettling detachment, an emotionless recall, as if it happened to a stranger on a screen.

The aftermath left Kwame profoundly altered. The constant, intrusive memory replay of the chaotic scene in the market made him constantly anticipate a similar attack, fueling a pervasive sense of threat. He became hypervigilant, his senses constantly on high alert, scanning every doorway and window. This intense vigilance made him feel unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the entire room, and he found himself scanning for exits as soon as he entered any building, even his own shop. This constant, exhausting monitoring for potential danger reinforced Kwame’s deeply held negative appraisals. He felt like he no longer belonged anywhere, isolated by his constant state of readiness, and this sustained fear solidified his belief that he was a weak person for being unable to overcome it.

The lingering memory gaps and the unsettling emotionless recall of crucial moments during the attack also made Kwame doubt his own competence and resilience. He began to believe, "I am a weak person," unable to fully process or even remember his own traumatic experience. His conviction that he couldn't trust that he would do the right thing extended even to his own mental processes, leading him to view his own recollections with suspicion, further contributing to the emotionless recall of certain parts, as if detaching from a memory he deemed unreliable or too dangerous to fully own.

To cope with the unbearable internal alarm bells, the pervasive sense of threat that compelled him to be superalert or watchful, Kwame found himself increasingly engaging in maladaptive strategies. He would spend long hours on his phone, playing games or browsing the internet, a form of screen escape, desperate to drown out the looping images and sounds of the memory replay. His belief that he was a weak person and that he couldn't trust that he would do the right thing made him feel utterly overwhelmed and hopeless. This hopelessness manifested as an inability to envision or commit to anything beyond the immediate, leading him to avoid making any plans for the future for his tailoring business, which had once been his passion. The constant tension from his hypervigilance also made him irritable, and he found himself seeking conflict, picking arguments or creating drama, almost as a perverse form of distraction from the internal pressure cooker.

Kwame's once-thriving tailor shop became a source of immense anxiety. He struggled to focus on intricate patterns, his mind always elsewhere, scanning for perceived threats. His avoidance of future plans meant he stopped investing in new fabrics or advertising, and his seeking conflict led to strained relationships with suppliers and even loyal customers, costing him business. He felt increasingly isolated, the belief that he no longer belonged anywhere becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy as he pushed people away. The cycles tightened: the intrusive memories fuelled his hypervigilance, which in turn reinforced his negative self-beliefs, driving him further into maladaptive coping that only served to keep the trauma alive. Exhausted and facing the potential collapse of his livelihood and his last remaining connections, Kwame finally sought help, fearing that he might never feel safe, or truly himself, again.
